meta.title: Old English Level 1
meta.subtitle: The 500 commonest words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Old English → English (see the Old English, recall the meaning) and English → Old English (see an English meaning, recall the Old English). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 500 words: the 500 commonest words of Old English prose. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: Old English has no examination and no graded word list, so a level here is a band of frequency, not a stage of conversation. The words were counted over about 112,000 words of Old English prose — Ælfric's Catholic Homilies (Thorpe's 1844 edition), the reading texts of Sweet's Anglo-Saxon Primer and Tatoeba's Old English sentences — by the WHOLE word, every form of a noun or a verb added together. Ælfric was a preacher and most surviving prose is religious, so God, Christ, heaven and the apostles come early; the vocabulary of the poetry is not here. Every headword is printed as modern editions and Wiktionary print it: a macron marks a long vowel (stān, 'stone') and a dot marks ċ and ġ where they are said 'ch' and 'y' (iċ, ġēar), with a reconstructed pronunciation in IPA beneath (8 words have none: Wiktionary gives none); the Old English Alphabet deck, the first in this collection, teaches how to read both. There is no speaker, because no voice reads Old English. The 192 nouns show their gender, genitive, plural and declension; the 136 verbs show their class and their principal parts — past, past plural, past participle — which is how a strong verb is learnt; the All forms fold holds the paradigm: a noun's four cases, a verb's present, past and subjunctive, and for the 43 adjectives the strong and the weak declension. THE TEXTS DO NOT SPELL AS THE DICTIONARY DOES: Wiktionary prints early West Saxon and Ælfric wrote late, so 52 cards carry a line, 'also in the texts', with the spellings the corpus really prints for that word (forþan for forþon, þisum for þissum) — only those Wiktionary itself files under the word. With them, the forms printed on these cards are 79% of all the running words of the corpus; another 12% are forms of words beyond this level, and 9% are names (Iohannes, Petrus) and spellings no dictionary entry matches — so about one word in five of a page of Ælfric is still to be looked up when this deck is done. 225 of the 500 words show their Modern English descendant where one survives (cyning → king), labelled as a descendant, not a translation. Sentences come with 477 of the 500 words, three apiece for 258 of them, the word picked out in colour and the source under each. On 415 cards at least one is Ælfric's own, in Thorpe's spelling — no macron, no dot, ð as often as þ, an acute here and there — with Thorpe's facing translation of 1844 and the page it stands on. The rest are Tatoeba's, by sentence number: written by that site's contributors in our own time, short and plain, and not evidence of the language. Sources. Meanings, gender, class, forms, pronunciation and descendants: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: counted by this deck's generator over B. Thorpe (ed.), The Homilies of the Anglo-Saxon Church, vol. 1 (1844) and H. Sweet, An Anglo-Saxon Primer, 8th ed. (1905), both public domain via Project Gutenberg, and Tatoeba. Example sentences: Thorpe's edition and translation (public domain) and Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR. THE BEGINNER PASS (November 2026). THE ORDER is frequency, the commonest word first — for a reader that is the order that reaches a page soonest — with one rule added: a small closed set arrives together, where its commonest member falls. So the first cards are sē · and · hē · hēo · hit; wesan and bēon, one verb in two stems, follow as notes 7 and 8; iċ, þū, wē and ġē come on day 13; willan, magan, sċulan, mōtan, cunnan and witan on day 17; mīn, þīn, ūre and ēower on day 18; the 7 question words on day 23; the numbers above one on day 34. No card was added and none removed: a level is a band of frequency, and by count six and nine are Level 2's (ranks 592 and 614), eight and ten Level 3's. THE PACE: the default is ten new cards a day, both directions together, which is five words a day; with the alphabet deck first, this deck runs from day 10 to day 110. WHAT A CARD SHOWS THAT IT DID NOT: sē has its whole table (þone, þæs, þām, þǣre — the card showed one form of thirty), bēon its present, 40 of the 43 adjectives the weak declension beside the strong, 179 of the 192 nouns their declension, and 52 cards the spellings Ælfric really uses. THE SENTENCES: 1,043 on 477 cards, 728 of them Ælfric's; on the day a card arrives 71% of the words of its sentences are forms a card has already shown, and 18% are on no card of this deck. WHERE THE SHELF ENDS: this is the last deck. Level 2, the next 500 words, is not built.
